h1: 10 Most Popular Attractions in Maha Sarakham
intro: Maha Sarakham is a quiet Isan city with treasures tucked away from the town center to the edge of the rice fields — an old wooden bridge stretching across a lake, the world's largest ordination hall built entirely of takhian wood, a white chedi marking the discovery of an ancient city, a thousand-year-old Khmer stone sanctuary, and a wide reservoir where you can cycle while watching the sunset. We've gathered the 10 attractions that visitors actually talk about most, with entry fees, locations, and trip-planning tips — do a one-day loop around town, or drive out to Na Dun for temples and ancient ruins on an overnight trip.
chips: 🌉 Kae Dam wooden bridge across the fields
🚲 Sunset cycling at Kaeng Loeng Chan
🐒 Monkey troops of Kosamphi Forest Park

blocks.html:
Maha Sarakham's charm is that of a laid-back university town whose best attractions are scattered across the whole province. In the city center, the City Pillar Shrine — dating back to 1865 — anchors local life, while Kaeng Loeng Chan, the wide reservoir behind Rajabhat Maha Sarakham University, draws people to walk, run, and cycle the roughly 10-kilometer loop around the water while watching the sunset. Come evening, Tonson Market lights up for a stroll through Isan street food. If your style leans spiritual or nature-loving, drive out to Kae Dam to walk the wooden bridge across the rice fields and stop at Wat Nong Hu Ling for Thailand's first boat-shaped ordination hall, head to Kosum Phisai to greet the monkey troops at Kosamphi Forest Park on the Chi River, or go south to Na Dun and collect a temple, a museum, and a stone sanctuary in a single trip. Temples and blessings, city life, nature, or history — it all links together.

This list includes the pins you shouldn't miss on a Maha Sarakham trip: Kae Dam Wooden Bridge, an old wooden bridge stretching more than 1 kilometer across a lake amid rice fields and lotus ponds that has become the province's signature photo spot; Wat Pa Wang Nam Yen in Koeng Subdistrict, home to what is said to be the world's largest ordination hall built entirely of golden takhian wood, with 32 takhian pillars, standing beside the great golden Chedi Si Maha Sarakham; and Phra Borommathat Na Dun, the large white chedi at the center of the Buddhist park, on the spot where evidence of the ancient city of Nakhon Champa Si and ancient clay votive tablets were unearthed. Not far away is Ku Santarat, a laterite sanctuary from the reign of King Jayavarman VII that remains in fairly complete condition and is free to visit. Scroll on for the details of each spot and plan your own route.

blocks.name: Kae Dam Wooden Bridge
blocks.signature: An old wooden bridge stretching more than 1 kilometer across Kae Dam lake, amid rice fields and lotus ponds, with a wooden window-frame photo corner and a frog statue
blocks.descHtml:
If you want to see a side of Maha Sarakham beyond the city, drive about 20 kilometers out toward Kae Dam district and stop at the Kae Dam Wooden Bridge at Wat Daowadueng, Ban Hua Khua. This old wooden bridge stretches across Kae Dam lake, connecting Ban Hua Khua with the village of Kae Dam on the other side. Villagers originally built it decades ago as a crossing over the reservoir, and from around 2015 it gradually became a hugely popular check-in spot. It suits anyone drawn to rice-field scenery, the quiet rhythms of rural Isan, and photographers hunting for an angle you won't find anywhere else.

The highlight is walking along the narrow wooden planks stretching far out over the water and lotus ponds, with green water and lotus leaves filling both sides. At the head of the bridge there's a charming wooden window frame set up as a photo prop, plus a giant frog statue — this area is famous for its frogs, a genuine local delicacy. Real reviews consistently say early morning or the hour before sunset gives the prettiest light and atmosphere, while midday is fairly punishing since there's no shade on the bridge.

Entry is free with no fees collected, and you can park along the roadside. Couples, families, and cyclists exploring the community can all stop by comfortably. At certain times the Ban Hua Khua community also sells local crafts — basketry, woven reed mats, and homestyle food — so a visit gives you both the photos and a genuine taste of village life.

One thing to know: the bridge itself is very old, some sections have deteriorated over the years, and repairs are made periodically. Walk carefully — planks can be slippery or damaged — go slowly, don't crowd together in one spot, and check the latest conditions before you go for peace of mind. But catch it at the right moment, with good light and the lake full, and this is one of Maha Sarakham's most classic views, worth seeing at least once.
mustOrder: Walk the long wooden bridge across the lake
The wooden window-frame photo corner
The giant frog statue at the bridgehead
Lotus ponds and the sunset
blocks.bestFor: Morning and evening light photography, community-style travel
blocks.hours: Open daily, all day (best in the morning and evening)

blocks.name: Wat Pa Wang Nam Yen
blocks.signature: Said to be the world's largest ordination hall built entirely of golden takhian wood, with 32 takhian pillars, alongside the great golden Chedi Si Maha Sarakham and a large wooden sermon hall with 112 pillars
blocks.descHtml:
If you can only visit one temple in Maha Sarakham, Wat Pa Wang Nam Yen (officially named Wat Phuttha Wanaram) is the answer most people give. This large forest monastery covers more than 30 rai at Ban Wang Nam Yen, Koeng Subdistrict, in Mueang district. Built and developed by Luang Pho Suriyan Khosapanyo, it has grown into a merit-making landmark that people from across Isan make a point of visiting. It suits temple-goers, admirers of wooden architecture, and families bringing older relatives for an easy stroll around a beautiful temple.

The unmissable highlight is the ordination hall built entirely of golden takhian wood, said to be the largest in the world, supported by 32 massive takhian pillars. Step inside and you can feel how detailed and grand the woodwork is — many reviewers say exactly the same thing, that "the wooden ordination hall is enormous" and looks nothing like an ordinary temple. It stands alongside the great golden Chedi Si Maha Sarakham, visible from far away, and a large wooden sermon hall raised on 112 pillars. Inside, a gold-adorned Buddha image is enshrined for paying respects and making wishes.

The atmosphere is shaded and peaceful in true forest-monastery style, pleasant for a slow photo walk — around 1–2 hours is just right. Best of all, entry is free with no admission fee, open daily roughly 06:00–18:30. Another favorite corner is the Café Amazon in front of the chedi, where you can sip coffee with a view of the temple.

Worth knowing: the midday Isan sun is fierce, and past visitors recommend coming in the morning or late afternoon for a more comfortable walk and better photos. Dress modestly, as this is an active temple with ceremonies and merit-makers coming through continuously. The temple was selected as one of the 25 Unseen New Chapters in 2023, so it's no surprise that holidays get crowded — arrive early for the best atmosphere.
mustOrder: The all-takhian-wood ordination hall (32 wooden pillars)
The great golden Chedi Si Maha Sarakham
The 112-pillar wooden sermon hall
Café Amazon in front of the chedi
blocks.bestFor: Merit-makers — temple visits and woodwork, best morning or evening
blocks.libCredit: Photo by Wiraphat Raksat / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

blocks.name: Phra Borommathat Na Dun
blocks.area: Phra That Subdistrict, Na Dun District, Maha Sarakham
blocks.signature: A great white chedi at the center of the Buddhist park, on the spot where evidence of the ancient city of Nakhon Champa Si and ancient clay votive tablets were unearthed, with an annual Phra Borommathat Na Dun homage festival
blocks.descHtml:
Phra Borommathat Na Dun is the great white chedi standing proudly over a wide plaza — the origin of the name "the Phutthamonthon of Isan" and one of Maha Sarakham's most sacred landmarks. This spot was once open rice-field land in Ban Na Dun until 1979, when villagers unearthed ancient clay votive tablets and a miniature stupa containing Buddha relics in a three-layered casket of gold, silver, and bronze — evidence of the ancient Dvaravati-era city of Nakhon Champa Si. Authorities then built the chedi over the site so people could pay their respects. It suits merit-makers, history lovers, and families looking for a stop on a southern-Isan route.

The thing not to miss is walking a circuit around the white chedi, which photographs beautifully from every angle — especially under a clear sky or in the soft late-afternoon light — then stopping at the nearby Nakhon Champa Si museum to see the original clay votive tablets. Most reviews agree the grounds are clean, spacious, shaded, and quiet — a good place to sit and settle your mind. Many give it full marks for the atmosphere and upkeep.

Entry is free with no admission fee, parking is convenient, and it's open daily roughly 07:00–18:00. The location is in Phra That Subdistrict, Na Dun District, about 65 km from Maha Sarakham city — driving yourself is easiest. Come in late February to early March and you'll catch the annual Phra Borommathat Na Dun homage festival, a big multi-day, multi-night event with mor lam performances, markets, and much larger crowds than usual.

It's popular because it combines sacredness, history, and photo spots in one place. Keep in mind that it is a sacred site — dress modestly — and the midday sun is strong across the open plaza, so bring an umbrella or hat and come in the morning or evening for comfort.
mustOrder: Walk a circuit around the great white chedi
See the ancient clay votive tablets at the Nakhon Champa Si museum
The annual Phra Borommathat Na Dun homage festival (Feb–Mar)
blocks.bestFor: Merit-makers and history lovers — pay respects in the morning or evening

blocks.name: Kaeng Loeng Chan
blocks.signature: A wide reservoir with a public park and a roughly 10 km loop road for walking, running, and cycling at sunset, with bike rentals and food stalls along the water
blocks.descHtml:
Kaeng Loeng Chan is a large reservoir on the western edge of Maha Sarakham city, behind Rajabhat Maha Sarakham University and only a few kilometers from the center — effectively the green lung and open-air gym for the whole province. The highlight is the roughly 10-kilometer road looping around the water, where people come to walk, run, and cycle almost every evening. It's ideal for nature lovers, families with kids who need room to run, and cyclists after a long waterside route. The embankment is landscaped as a public park, with flower gardens, rest pavilions, and a pavilion over the water where you can sit and catch the breeze.

The thing not to miss is the sunset over the reservoir — review after review says the evening sky reflecting across the water is gorgeous, making it a favorite photo spot. Didn't bring a bike? Rent one cheaply for around 20 baht from local community groups, and there are food stalls along the water for refueling after a ride. The overall atmosphere is shaded with plenty of big trees and never feels like a commercialized attraction — most people here are locals exercising or picnicking with family.

No need to worry about costs, because entry is free and the area is open at all hours, though the most popular times are early morning around 6 a.m. and the hour before sunset. It sits in Kaeng Loeng Chan Subdistrict, Mueang Maha Sarakham, next to the bypass road — easy to reach by car or motorbike, with wide parking areas. Running and cycling events are held here at times, especially in the cool season when the weather is at its best.

Before you go: facilities are still simple — toilets are limited and shops are few, so bring some water and snacks. If you plan to ride the full loop, allow enough time and avoid the midday sun. In the rainy season some stretches can be slippery and the water can run high — checking the weather first is your best bet. Come in the morning or evening and you'll get the best of it.
mustOrder: Cycle, run, or walk the ~10 km loop road
Watch the sunset over the reservoir
Rent a bike cheaply for ~20 baht
Sit in the over-water pavilion and flower gardens on the embankment
blocks.bestFor: Walkers, runners, and sunset cyclists — plus family picnics, morning and evening
blocks.zone: West of the city (behind Rajabhat Maha Sarakham University)
blocks.hours: Open daily (public area, accessible at all hours)

blocks.name: Wat Nong Hu Ling (Ananta Nakkharat Merit-Boat Ordination Hall)
blocks.signature: A boat-shaped ordination hall, the "Ananta Nakkharat," said to be Thailand's first boat ubosot
blocks.descHtml:
If you think a temple's ordination hall has to be a rectangular building with tiered roofs like every one you've seen, Wat Nong Hu Ling in Kae Dam district will stop you in your tracks — its ubosot is built as a great golden "boat" wrapped by the naga Ananta Nakkharat. Locals simply call it "the boat temple," and it's often said to be the first boat-shaped ordination hall in Thailand. The merit boat took around ten years to build, funded bit by bit through donations from the faithful — so it isn't just a work of architecture, it's devotion taking shape a little at a time.

The charm is in the details, each placed with a lesson in mind. The abbot designed the hall himself, and every element carries meaning — from the entrance you walk beneath, symbolizing letting go of what weighs on your mind, to the boat itself, representing the passage out of suffering. Inside, the hall enshrines a Buddha image in the First Sermon posture, as if inviting everyone who steps in to sit and quietly listen to the teachings. The naga figures and stucco work around the boat are finely done — circling the hall with a camera is genuinely enjoyable, especially in the soft morning or evening light when the gold catches the sun.

The overall atmosphere is that of a quiet countryside temple, nothing like the crowded famous temples of big cities. It suits anyone who wants to pay respects, photograph unusual architecture, or take an unhurried Isan road trip. If you enjoy traditional merit festivals, people often mention the candlelight processions around the boat-shaped hall on important Buddhist days — a sight you won't see often.

For getting there: the temple is in Mittraphap Subdistrict, Kae Dam District, an easy drive from Maha Sarakham city on a day trip. Dress modestly since it's a religious site, allow a little time to walk around the boat, and if you go inside to pay respects, remove your shoes and observe temple etiquette. It's a stop that rounds out a Maha Sarakham trip with something more unexpected than you'd think.
mustOrder: The golden Ananta Nakkharat boat-shaped ordination hall
The naga wrapped around the hull
The First Sermon Buddha image inside the hall
Photo angles in the soft morning and evening light
blocks.bestFor: Temple visits and photographing unusual architecture

blocks.title: 🛏️ Maha Sarakham stays — sleep in town near Kaeng Loeng Chan and Tonson Market
blocks.text: To get the most out of Maha Sarakham, try staying a night. You can cycle along Kaeng Loeng Chan in the evening, graze on Isan street food at Tonson Market, then drive out in the morning to pay respects at the takhian-wood ordination hall of Wat Pa Wang Nam Yen or head down to Na Dun before the crowds arrive. The most popular stays cluster in Maha Sarakham city near Mahasarakham University and Tonson Market, with easy access to the sights around town — both city-center hotels and places near the university. Pick a location close to your first stop of the morning for the best value, and compare prices and reviews before booking.

blocks.name: Tonson Market
blocks.signature: A night market with pretty lighting, wide walkways, and plenty of street food — well-known stalls and evening snacks — plus a central seating zone with a big screen showing live football
blocks.descHtml:
Tonson Market is the night market in the heart of Maha Sarakham, in Talat Subdistrict within the municipal area, and it has become the city's default evening meeting point. Its strengths are the pretty lighting, wide walkways that never feel cramped, and the fact that every stall is covered against sun and rain — even in a downpour you can keep eating and browsing. It works with friends, with a date, with the whole family, or as a solo dinner run after work. Parking is plentiful and getting there is easy.

The highlight everyone talks about is the central seating zone with a big screen showing live football — if your idea of a good evening is sitting back with a beer, live music, and a match while you eat, this is the answer. Well-known stalls like Nai Tong mookata even arrange their tables so you can see the screen. The most-praised snack is the cheese tea — pleasantly sweet rather than cloying, richly cheesy, and friendly on the wallet — and there's properly spicy Isan food like pon kop (frog chili dip) to try too. One lap around covers savory dishes, desserts, and shopping for clothes, bags, and shoes.

Costs are easy: the market is free to enter and you pay only for what you eat — a few hundred baht fills you up. The atmosphere starts to pick up in the early evening, and after dark the crowd grows and more stalls are open. It runs daily — the night market zone from about 16:00 until midnight, and the community market zone from afternoon to early evening.

Worth knowing: during festivals or the rainy season the market sometimes adjusts its hours, so a quick check of its Facebook page before leaving home is worth it. And if you're coming to watch a big football match, claim a table in front of the screen early in the evening because it fills up. The market's reputation has grown fast, making it the city's night-market landmark in just a few years.
mustOrder: Nai Tong mookata (with a view of the football screen)
Cheese tea — pleasantly sweet, friendly price
Pon kop and other spicy Isan dishes
The central zone's big screen with live football
blocks.bestFor: Dinner into late evening — chilling with friends over football

blocks.name: Kosamphi Forest Park
blocks.area: Hua Khwang Subdistrict, Kosum Phisai District, Maha Sarakham
blocks.cuisine: Forest park / Riverside forest on the Chi River
blocks.signature: Natural evergreen forest on the Chi River, with hundreds of long-tailed macaques waiting to greet you, plus nature trails and the Kaeng Tat rapids viewpoint — great for feeding the monkeys and strolling
blocks.descHtml:
Kosamphi Forest Park is a patch of evergreen forest of around 125 rai on the Chi River, only about 28 kilometers from Maha Sarakham city — under half an hour's drive. Its claim to fame is the troop of several hundred long-tailed macaques that come out to greet you right from the entrance, and — more unusual still — golden-coated macaques that several sources say can be found only here in the Asia-Pacific. It's a great fit for families bringing kids to see the monkeys, nature lovers after a shaded forest walk, and anyone wanting a free outing near the city that needs no elaborate planning.

Don't miss buying bananas or nuts to feed the monkeys (guard your valuables and plastic bags — the monkeys are quick), walking the nature-study trail — a concrete path you can comfortably walk or cycle through the forest — crossing the suspension bridge over the pond in the middle of the park for photos, and heading to the Kaeng Tat rapids on the Chi River, which become a popular swimming spot in the dry season. Before going in to see the monkeys, locals traditionally stop to pay respects to Luang Pho Ming Mueang, the revered Buddha image at the entrance.

Inside, the shade comes from big trees — yang na, tako, and khoi — and the walk feels cool, like slipping out of the heat and into the forest. Entry is free with no ticket, open daily around 08:00–18:00. Reviewers recommend late afternoon into early evening, when the monkeys come out in numbers and are livelier — at hot midday they hide from the sun and you'll see far fewer.

Things to know: the monkeys here are used to people and fairly mischievous — watch whatever is in your hands, plus glasses, phones, and food bags; don't tease them or get close to mothers with infants. Late in the rainy season the Chi River can flood parts of the park, sending the monkeys up into the trees, so checking the weather before you go is safer. All told, it's a free outing near the city that combines monkey-watching, a forest walk, and a riverside break in one place — which is why it has been Kosum Phisai's signature attraction for so long.
mustOrder: Feed the macaque troop at the entrance
Look for the rare golden-coated macaques
Walk or cycle the nature trail + suspension bridge
See the Kaeng Tat rapids on the Chi River
blocks.bestFor: Nature lovers and families — late afternoon to feed the monkeys and walk the forest

blocks.name: Maha Sarakham City Pillar Shrine
blocks.signature: A city pillar shrine dating to 1865 and the era of the city's first governor — the town's spiritual anchor and central spot for making wishes
blocks.descHtml:
If you've arrived in Maha Sarakham and want to start the trip on an auspicious note, the City Pillar Shrine is the first stop locals like to recommend. It sits dead center in town on Nakhon Sawan Road, near Lak Mueang Maha Sarakham School, and serves as the spiritual anchor and wish-making spot for the whole province. What makes it special is a history reaching back to 1865 and the era of Phra Charoen Ratchadet (Thao Kuat), the city's first governor, who led settlers from Roi Et to found the new town and built the shrine of the city pillar's guardian spirit as its sacred heart. It suits the spiritually inclined, anyone wishing for luck in work or fortune, and travelers who collect each province's historic landmarks.

The highlight not to miss is the city pillar itself, carved from chaiyaphruek wood, lacquered and gilded — genuinely beautiful — enshrined in a four-porticoed pavilion with stairways on all four sides, so you can circle the pillar as you pay respects. At the entrance, flower-and-incense sets are sold for a few dozen baht for anyone who wants to make a wish. Many people come here to fulfill vows or ask for help with important matters. During the annual Bun Boek Fa festival and Red Cross fair, a grand ceremony honors the pillar's guardian spirits and the shrine is especially lively.

The grounds around the shrine are more pleasant than you might expect — frangipani trees ring the plaza, there are benches to rest on, and everything is kept clean and tidy. Real reviews agree the building itself is modest and unassuming, and a full visit takes under an hour — so it works better as a short stop en route than a long stay. Some people come as early as 6 a.m., just as the grounds are being swept and the shrine opens, when the air is at its most comfortable.

Entry is free, with worship hours roughly 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. daily. Street parking is easy to find since it's right in the middle of town, close to markets and food streets for an easy onward walk. The only note is that it's a sacred site — dress modestly and be composed when paying respects. It's popular precisely because it sits mid-town where anyone passing can drop in, and because it's tied directly to the founding of Maha Sarakham — if you're in the province, it's worth a visit at least once.
mustOrder: Pay respects to the carved, lacquered and gilded chaiyaphruek city pillar
Make a wish to the city pillar guardian spirit
Walk the four-porticoed pavilion with stairways on all four sides
Rest under the frangipani trees around the plaza
blocks.bestFor: First stop of the trip — make a wish in the town center before heading elsewhere

blocks.name: Isan House Museum, Mahasarakham University
blocks.area: Mahasarakham University (Walai Rukhavej station, Na Dun)
blocks.signature: A museum of wooden houses showcasing traditional Isan life and vernacular architecture, with historic houses and original household objects to walk through and learn from
blocks.descHtml:
If you want to understand how Isan people lived 40–50 years ago, the Isan House Museum at Mahasarakham University's Walai Rukhavej research station shows you in a way you can actually picture. This isn't a museum of chilled glass cases — it's a cluster of real wooden houses relocated and arranged in shaded woodland: an Isan house, a Phu Thai house, a Yo house, each set up as a "living museum" where you can climb up and inspect the household objects for real. It's excellent for culture lovers, anyone curious about rural life, and families who want the kids to see the real thing outside their textbooks.

The highlight not to miss is walking from house to house, because each one tells a different story — from kitchenware, earthen jars, and pots to rice-farming tools and a traditional weaving loom that took several pairs of hands to operate. Around the grounds are a cart shed, a rice-field hut, haystacks, and model rice paddies, giving you the complete picture of an old Isan village. Past visitors consistently mention the shade of the big trees and how warmly nostalgic the photos come out.

Budget is no concern, because entry is free, open daily around 08:00–16:00. The museum sits within the Walai Rukhavej station in Na Dun district, close to Phra That Na Dun, so people commonly pair the two — pay respects at the chedi, then wander the Isan houses in the same outing. That's one reason it's such a well-known cultural stop for anyone visiting Maha Sarakham.

A few small things to know: the grounds are fairly spread out and the houses are open-air, so come in the morning or late afternoon to avoid the midday sun, and wear comfortable shoes since you'll be walking and climbing wooden stairs. At times it can be very quiet with no guide on hand, so if you're coming as a group, call the Walai Rukhavej Research Institute ahead to get the most out of the visit.
mustOrder: The cluster of traditional houses — Isan, Phu Thai, and Yo houses set up as a living museum
Original household objects, from kitchenware and farming tools to a weaving loom
The cart shed, field hut, haystacks, and model rice paddies around the grounds
The shaded Walai Rukhavej woodland — pairs easily with Phra That Na Dun
blocks.bestFor: Culture lovers learning Isan folkways — continue on from Phra That Na Dun
blocks.zone: Na Dun / Phra That Na Dun

blocks.name: Ku Santarat
blocks.signature: A laterite Khmer sanctuary (an arokayasala hospital chapel) built in the reign of King Jayavarman VII, in fairly complete condition, free to visit, and easy to pair with Phra That Na Dun
blocks.descHtml:
Ku Santarat (sometimes called Ku Non Mueang) is a laterite Khmer sanctuary hidden among the fields of Ban Ku Non Mueang, Ku Santarat Subdistrict, Na Dun District, about 4 kilometers from the district town. It was one of the "arokayasala," or royal hospital chapels, built in the reign of King Jayavarman VII around the 18th Buddhist century (roughly 1157–1207 CE). If you're drawn to the atmosphere of ancient Khmer history and quiet walks through the traces of the Nakhon Champa Si civilization, this is an excellent spot — it's far less busy than the famous sanctuaries of lower Isan, so you can wander at your own pace without competing for photo angles.

The highlight is the main prang, square in plan and facing east, built up in courses of laterite, with a real doorway on the east side and false doors on the other three. A laterite wall surrounds it, and a pond or "baray" of roughly 10 by 12 meters sits at the northeast corner, following the classic Khmer approach to water management. What many visitors notice, echoed in reviews, is how relatively complete the sanctuary looks compared with other ku in the area — yet the lintel carvings and decorative colonettes were never finished, believed left incomplete since ancient times, which gives the place a raw, bare-stone character that's a charm of its own.

The Fine Arts Department registered it as a national monument back in 1935. Today it's free to visit with no ticket, open during the day roughly 08:00–18:00. The grounds are an open, sunlit clearing, so morning or late afternoon is best for photos and comfort. The clincher is the location — only a few kilometers from Phra Borommathat Na Dun, making a combined day trip easy. Many people pay respects at the chedi and then visit Ku Santarat and Ku Noi as a set.

Things to know: this is an open-air monument with no shops or cafés on site, so bring your own water and a hat. The access road is fairly narrow but passable by sedan; there is some signage, but keep GPS on. And please help keep the site clean and don't climb on the sanctuary, so future generations can see the real thing too.
mustOrder: The laterite main prang from the reign of King Jayavarman VII
The east doorway + 3 false doors
The baray pond (at the northeast corner)
Continue on to Phra Borommathat Na Dun
blocks.bestFor: Morning-to-noon visits paired with Phra That Na Dun — for history lovers

blocks.title: What to know before visiting Maha Sarakham

items.title: Driving yourself or renting is easiest
items.text: The in-town sights sit close together, but Kae Dam Wooden Bridge, Kosamphi Forest Park, and Phra Borommathat Na Dun are out of town in different directions. Public transport is limited and Grab coverage in Maha Sarakham is very thin. The most practical option is renting a car or a motorbike — have your transport sorted before heading out of town.

items.title: Carry cash
items.text: Food at Tonson Market, bike rentals at Kaeng Loeng Chan, flower-and-incense sets at the City Pillar Shrine, and most temple donation boxes run on cash. Keep small bills for roadside food and parking fees. ATMs are easy to find in town but scarce at the out-of-town sights.

items.title: Do the wooden bridge and Kaeng Loeng Chan in the evening
items.text: Midday in Maha Sarakham is fiercely sunny. Visit Kae Dam Wooden Bridge and Kaeng Loeng Chan in the morning or near sunset for better photos and a more comfortable walk. Tonson Market only runs from late afternoon into the night, so plan your timing if a food walk is the goal.

items.title: Dress modestly at temples
items.text: Wat Pa Wang Nam Yen, Phra Borommathat Na Dun, and Ku Santarat are sacred places where people genuinely come to worship. Cover shoulders and knees, remove shoes where signs indicate, and keep your voice low around the ordination halls and the chedi. At the City Pillar Shrine, flower-and-incense sets sell for roughly 20–50 baht.

items.title: Watch your valuables when feeding the monkeys
items.text: Kosamphi Forest Park has hundreds of long-tailed macaques waiting to greet you. It's fun, but the monkeys are fairly mischievous — stow glasses, hats, plastic bags, and snacks out of sight, hold food out to them carefully, and don't tease them or get too close to infant monkeys.

items.title: English is limited
items.text: Outside the Mahasarakham University area, English signs and menus are rare. Carry a translation app, or simply point at pictures at Tonson Market and Isan restaurants — it works. As a university town, the younger crowd can usually help communicate and are friendly to visitors.

blocks.title: Plan a Maha Sarakham trip that covers the most
blocks.html:
Maha Sarakham is easy to plan because the in-town highlights sit close together. In the morning, make a wish at the City Pillar Shrine in the old town, then stop at Wat Pa Wang Nam Yen in Koeng Subdistrict for the all-takhian-wood ordination hall and the great Chedi Si Maha Sarakham. In the afternoon, head to Kaeng Loeng Chan behind the Rajabhat university, rent a bike for the roughly 10-kilometer loop, and wait for the sunset. Finish the evening at Tonson Market grazing on Isan street food — one day covers everything in town.

With more than a day, drive out of town. Photographers should head to Kae Dam to walk the kilometer-plus wooden bridge across the rice fields and lotus ponds in the soft morning or evening light, then stop at Wat Nong Hu Ling for the boat-shaped ordination hall in the same district. Nature-minded families can take the kids to Kosamphi Forest Park in Kosum Phisai to feed the macaques and stroll along the Chi River. And for the spiritually and historically inclined, drive south to Na Dun and collect Phra Borommathat Na Dun, MSU's Isan House Museum, and Ku Santarat — the Khmer stone sanctuary in the same zone — all in one go. Bundling the Na Dun stops into a single loop saves the most time.

blocks.text: Maha Sarakham is fun even as a day trip, but stay a night in town and you can cycle along Kaeng Loeng Chan at sunset, graze on Isan food at Tonson Market, then drive out in the morning to the takhian-wood ordination hall or down to Na Dun for the chedi and the stone sanctuary. faq.q: What are the must-see attractions in Maha Sarakham?
faq.a: The pins visitors don't miss are Kae Dam Wooden Bridge, an old wooden bridge stretching more than 1 kilometer across a lake and rice fields in Kae Dam district; Wat Pa Wang Nam Yen in Koeng Subdistrict, home to what is said to be the world's largest all-takhian-wood ordination hall and the great Chedi Si Maha Sarakham; Phra Borommathat Na Dun, the great white chedi at the center of the Buddhist park in Na Dun district; Kaeng Loeng Chan, the wide reservoir behind the Rajabhat university where people cycle at sunset; Wat Nong Hu Ling in Kae Dam, with Thailand's first boat-shaped ordination hall; and Ku Santarat, a thousand-year-old Khmer stone sanctuary.

faq.q: What are the highlights of Maha Sarakham?
faq.a: Maha Sarakham's highlights are things you won't find anywhere else: the world's largest ordination hall built entirely of golden takhian wood at Wat Pa Wang Nam Yen, with 32 takhian pillars and a 112-pillar wooden sermon hall; Kae Dam Wooden Bridge, stretching more than 1 kilometer across a lake amid rice fields and lotus ponds; and Phra Borommathat Na Dun, the white chedi marking the spot where evidence of the ancient city of Nakhon Champa Si and ancient clay votive tablets were unearthed — paired with Ku Santarat, a laterite sanctuary from the reign of King Jayavarman VII in the same zone.

faq.q: Are entry fees expensive in Maha Sarakham?
faq.a: Most attractions are free or nearly so. Kae Dam Wooden Bridge, Wat Pa Wang Nam Yen, Phra Borommathat Na Dun, Kosamphi Forest Park, the City Pillar Shrine, the Isan House Museum, Wat Nong Hu Ling, and Ku Santarat are all free to enter. Kaeng Loeng Chan is free, with bike rental around 20 baht; Tonson Market is free to enter, with food costing roughly 80–200 baht per person. Wat Nong Hu Ling is free, with donations at your discretion.

faq.q: How do you get to Maha Sarakham, and is parking convenient?
faq.a: Maha Sarakham has no airport of its own — most people take a coach from Bangkok or fly to Khon Kaen or Roi Et and continue by road. Once there, driving yourself or renting a car is by far the most convenient option, since public transport within the province is limited. The in-town sights — the City Pillar Shrine, Kaeng Loeng Chan, and Tonson Market — sit close together with parking lots, while Kae Dam Wooden Bridge and Wat Nong Hu Ling in Kae Dam, Kosamphi Forest Park in Kosum Phisai, and Phra Borommathat Na Dun and Ku Santarat in Na Dun lie out of town in different directions — sort out your transport before leaving the city.

faq.q: What time do Maha Sarakham's attractions open?
faq.a: Temples and monuments such as Wat Pa Wang Nam Yen, Phra Borommathat Na Dun, and Ku Santarat open through the day into early evening — mornings are quieter and cooler. Kae Dam Wooden Bridge and Kaeng Loeng Chan are prettiest in the morning or near sunset. Tonson Market runs evenings into the night only. Wat Nong Hu Ling opens during the day into early evening, and Kosamphi Forest Park opens in the daytime. Check each place's hours before setting out, as they can shift on holidays.
